NextItNet’s causal dilated convolutions expand the historical receptive field; residual blocks support deeper optimization. These provide natural intervention sites for diagnosing recency dependence and long-range signal loss ([original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163)). Relevant 2024 interpretability work supports activation patching but stresses that conclusions depend on corruption choice, intervention direction and output metric ([patching guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15255)). This is methodological transfer from language models, not established NextItNet-specific evidence.

A bounded adaptation: reuse one frozen checkpoint per category, read the final nonpadding position, fix the highest-scoring negative competitor, and differentiate the margin s(positive)−s(competitor) with respect to residual-branch activations. Compare gradient-predicted effects with actual small branch-scaling interventions or clean/corrupted activation replacements. Include identity patches, equal-norm random perturbations and matched history corruptions; keep padding, candidate sets and competitor identity fixed within each comparison. These controls are proposed adaptations. [AtP* (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00745) identifies false negatives in gradient approximations to activation patching, supporting direct intervention checks before interpreting low attribution as irrelevance.

Report signed margin changes, positive rank and paired HR@10 changes separately. Component sensitivity establishes dependence under the tested intervention; it does not establish that modifying or retraining that component improves recommendation accuracy. [A Fresh Look at Sanity Checks (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.02383) further warns that attribution-evaluation noise and similarity metrics can distort conclusions. Accuracy claims therefore require the unchanged macro validation protocol; attribution magnitude alone is insufficient.
